entries.title: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
entries.summary: Engineers from Amazon Web Services (AWS) have described how the team that maintains the Linux kernel for EC2 infrastructure handles kernel CVEs. The process combines an automated filter, an AI agent and human review. The team also argues that it needs to move to newer long-term-support (LTS) kernels, as older branches collect fixes that are never backported. By Matt Saunders
entries.content:
Engineers from Amazon Web Services (AWS) have described how the team that maintains the Linux kernel for EC2 infrastructure handles kernel CVEs. The process combines an automated filter, an AI agent and human review. The team also argues that it needs to move to newer long-term-support (LTS) kernels, as older branches collect fixes that are never backported.

Dylan Johnson and Justinien Bouron gave the talk at the Linux Plumbers Conference in Prague earlier this month. At the start of the recording, Johnson explains that the team maintains the kernel used within EC2 infrastructure. This is separate from Amazon Linux and from the kernels that customers run in their virtual machines.

After the kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority in February 2024, the team saw about two kernel CVEs a week before 2024 and about 16 a day afterwards, with 848 published on 15 August 2026. The kernel CVE documentation states that the project cannot know how a given system uses the kernel, so users must decide which CVEs apply to them.

The first stage of AWS's process does not use AI. Bouron explained that kernel CVE records are published in JSON and list the affected versions and source files. A script discards a CVE if the kernel version is outside the affected range, or if none of the listed files are built into the image. In AWS's environment this removes about 70% of CVEs, although Bouron said the figure depends heavily on kernel configuration.

The remaining CVEs go to an AI agent. It receives AWS's kernel source tree, the configuration for each platform, a description of the environment and threat model, and a severity rubric. The agent produces a table that records the affected subsystem, the vulnerability type and the attack vector. Bouron said the team ignores CVSS scores, because they are not specific to its environment.

"We're really using it as a very fancy classifier."

Dylan Johnson

Two engineers usually review the table. According to the slides, the agent needs about 3.4 seconds per CVE, compared with minutes for a person. Bouron said review is now the slowest step in the process, and that the team does not intend to remove it.

"We don't want to hinge our entire security posture on the output of an LLM agent."

Justinien Bouron

When asked about accuracy, Bouron estimated that between 5% and 10% of the agent's decisions were problematic. This was an informal estimate, and the talk did not describe a formal evaluation.

The team also disabled kernel features it did not need, to reduce the number of applicable CVEs. Bouron called this approach "deceptively difficult". The slides list more than 32,000 configuration options, and removing the wrong one can cause bugs or performance regressions that appear months later.

The team's data also shows that older LTS branches receive fixes later and carry more unfixed CVEs. For CVEs affecting all six branches studied, the median time from a mainline fix to an LTS release was 31.8 days for Linux 5.10 and 18.1 days for 6.18. On 16 September, 1,709 known CVEs were unfixed in 5.10, compared with 229 in 6.18. These are counts for each branch, and they do not show how many affect AWS's own kernel.

Backporting fixes in-house brings its own risks. Bouron pointed out that CVE records often name only the final fixing commit. A team that misses the prerequisite commits may still be vulnerable after applying the listed fix.

AWS has shortened its own upgrades. Johnson said the move from 4.19 to 5.10 took about two years, measured from the start of porting work to full production deployment. The next upgrade took about a year, and the move to 6.18 took about six months. During the 5.10-to-6.12 upgrade, 43% of tracked issues were fixed in userspace, where workloads depended on older kernel behaviour. Johnson said the team will now run stable kernels in testing through the year, and move the fleet when each new LTS release appears.

Microsoft's Azure Linux team described a similar pipeline at the same conference. Its triage verdicts come from a rule table, and AI only suggests inputs to it. The team uses agents for backporting, and reported that a build-and-test feedback loop raised its success rate from about 50% to 80%. Google DeepMind's CodeMender, which InfoQ covered in October 2025, focuses on writing fixes. Its announcement stated that human researchers review every patch before it is submitted upstream.

Berend de Boer, CTO of Process Focus, commented on LinkedIn about the work involved in running cloud infrastructure. He listed host patching and Linux CVEs among the work that organisations take on when they build their own cloud. "Focus on what makes your business valuable to your customers," he wrote.

AWS has not released the tools. Asked about open-sourcing them, Johnson said the team would like to explore sharing the filtering tool. He also acknowledged that AWS's internal users make it easier to disable features than it would be for a general-purpose distribution.

entries.title: Cloudflare and VoidZero Introduce tsrs: An AI-Generated Rust Port of TypeScript
entries.summary: Cloudflare, VoidZero and Max Schwenk announced tsrs, an experimental Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, built with the TypeScript team's involvement. Cloudflare claims up to 8x faster checking and 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0, though one test against 7.1 beta showed 2.7x. It lacks watch mode and a language server, and exits with code 2 on type errors. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, has been announced by Cloudflare, which is developing it with VoidZero and Max Schwenk of Owner.com, incubating the project inside the Oxc toolchain and working in close collaboration with the TypeScript team. Cloudflare is emphatic that this is not a fork, with the TypeScript team retaining full control over the language's design.

Cloudflare's benchmark comparing tsrs against TypeScript 7.0 at the same number of checker workers

The headline numbers are a claimed up to 8x faster type checking and around 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0 at the same number of checker workers. Rust also unlocks the use case of compiling to WebAssembly through @tsrs/wasm so checks can run in a browser or on Workers, without dragging a garbage collector into the bundle the way a Go binary does.

To try, developers simply point it at an existing tsconfig and run:

npm install -D tsrs
npx tsrs -p . --noEmit

In a detailed write-up, Schwenk explains he wrote "zero" code, instead directing agents led by Claude Opus 5.5 to produce a faithful port, using TypeScript's own 15,197 conformance cases as the spec. On Owner's 37,000-file monolith, a check that needed 19 GiB and 80 seconds on TypeScript 7.0 dropped to 7 seconds.

One developer benchmarked both npm packages and measured 5.3x faster checking and 72% less memory, with identical diagnostics and byte-identical emit, but spotted that tsrs exits with code 2 on type errors where tsc exits 1, enough to quietly break a CI script. Measuring against the newer TypeScript 7.1 beta rather than 7.0, ImportStatic found a smaller 2.7x gain, a reminder that the 8x headline is measured against the older baseline.

TypeScript's Daniel Rosenwasser responded that much of the speed "does not just come down to language choice," and that some optimisations discovered in tsrs are feeding into a leaner TypeScript 7.1. Peter Steinberger reported on X:

Moved to tsrs over the weekend. Drop-in replacement. Around 5x faster for OC.

Kind of amazing that it took Microsoft a team and two years to rewrite the TS compiler in go, and now you can just let an agent rip and get sth significantly better within weeks.

Others were wary, questioning whether the arena-based, never-freed memory model is sound.

tsrs sits alongside Microsoft's own Go-based compiler, known as tsgo, and Theo Browne's rival Rust port, 

tsc-rs
. Rather than compete, Cloudflare is merging tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package, adding language server and content mapper support.

The release remains experimental. There is no watch mode or language server yet, 

--init
and 
--showConfig
are unsupported, and diagnostic order can differ, the compatibility notes provide more details. Because tsrs tracks TypeScript 7, teams still on TypeScript 5 or 6 should first adopt Microsoft's native Go port before swapping in tsrs, after which migrating is as simple as reusing the existing tsconfig.

tsrs is open source under Apache-2.0 and available on GitHub.

entries.title: Developers Reporting Double-Digit Weekly Time Savings from AI Fell from 68% to 26%
entries.summary: Atlassian’s State of Developer Experience 2026 finds the share of developers saving ten or more hours a week with AI dropped from 68% to 26% year over year, while only 28% report noticeably less friction than before AI. Engineering leaders report spending more time managing and correcting AI output than developers do. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
entries.content:
The share of developers reporting ten or more hours saved each week through AI fell from 68% to 26% in a year, according to Atlassian’s State of Developer Experience 2026. Adoption over the same period became close to universal, with 95% of developers and 96% of engineering leaders saying their organization actively uses AI in engineering.

The report draws on 1,155 individual contributors and 405 engineering leaders surveyed during 2026. Atlassian is unusually direct about what that means, stating that its findings "reflect self-reported experience and perception, not system-level telemetry such as deployment frequency, cycle time, or revenue impact," and that associations in the data "should not be interpreted as causal proof."

Taroon Mandhana, Atlassian’s CTO for AI and Teamwork, summarised the shift as one where "the bottleneck has moved to managing AI’s work."

Local benefit has not gone away. Eighty-seven percent of developers say AI helps them ship faster and 80% say it helps them deliver more without longer hours. What has not followed is relief from everyday obstacles. Only 28% report noticeably less friction than before AI, while 50% report about the same amount, which the report describes as friction "of a different type than before AI."

Some of that difference is AI itself. Forty-nine percent of developers now spend four or more hours a week managing AI tools, and 65% say they spend time correcting AI-generated work that missed the original intent. Both figures run higher among engineering leaders, at 57% and 72%. Twenty-nine percent name reviewing or managing AI-generated code as a source of friction outright.

The rest of the list has barely moved in three years. Finding information leads at 51%, followed by meetings at 50%, context switching at 45% and technical debt at 44%. Finding information also topped the 2025 list and placed second in 2024. Coding has never appeared on it.

Measurement is where the report is most pointed. Sixty percent of developers say AI use is treated as a productivity signal in their organization, 41% say they sometimes use AI more than necessary because they feel expected to, and only 42% of leaders say they have the right metrics to separate real gains from activity.

Responding to Mandhana, Shan Huang, who builds production AI agents for enterprise workflows, connected two of those figures:

If people are using AI more than necessary because they feel expected to, part of that 49% spending 4+ hours a week managing AI output is not a tooling problem, it is a metric problem. Call it performative throughput: the usage gets counted as productivity, and the cleanup lands on somebody else’s calendar.

Taylor Johnson of Athena Intelligence proposed a replacement in one line:

AI activity is not impact; measure accepted work, not usage.

Organizations with a stated position are rare and appear to fare better. Seventeen percent of developers and 23% of leaders report a clear, actively implemented AI strategy across the software delivery lifecycle. Among developers who do, 41% report noticeably less friction than before AI, against 22% of those describing an inconsistent or poorly communicated strategy. Andrew Boyagi, Atlassian’s head of DevOps evangelism, calls that gap the differentiator, though the report itself cautions that the association is not causal.

One trend has run the same way for three years. The share of developers saying leadership does not fully understand the challenges they face was 44% in 2024, 63% in 2025, and 66% in 2026.

Cam Turner, a designer and former AWS staffer, put the practical question that neither the report nor the thread answered: "68 to 26 in a year says the work moved from making to reviewing. Is anyone designing the review step yet, or are teams just absorbing it?"

Two caveats sit on the headline figure. This is vendor research from a company selling developer tooling, landing on a conclusion that favors formalizing AI delivery. The comparison base also changed, from 3,500 developers and managers across six countries in 2025 to 1,560 respondents this year, and neither edition publishes fieldwork dates.

Self-reported hours are soft in both directions, which commenter Harshit Jain raised directly: is the drop about review load, or about higher expectations? The report does not separate them.

entries.title: AGNTCon + MCPCon 2026: Agentic AI Foundation Adds Four Projects as MCP Turns to Security
entries.summary: At AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026, the Agentic AI Foundation added OpenSandbox, Open Responses, Agent Skills, and OpenEnv, reaching ten projects in its first year. Keynotes from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and UC Berkeley focused on MCP in production, security, and agents with their own identities. By Andrew Hoblitzell
entries.content:
At AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 in San Jose, the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) added four projects, taking it from three founding projects to ten in its first year. The October 22-23 event followed PyTorch Conference at the same venue, and much of its program moved from new protocol features to security and identity.

Mazin Gilbert, executive director of the AAIF, opened with the project news and three new governance committees. Alibaba contributed OpenSandbox, a secure sandbox for running agents, and OpenAI contributed Open Responses, an open specification for interoperable LLM interfaces. Anthropic added Agent Skills, and Hugging Face added OpenEnv, a framework for reinforcement learning environments that train and evaluate agents. Manik Surtani, the foundation's CTO, put the milestone this way in the announcement:

A year ago, AAIF launched with three projects and a bet that agentic AI needed a neutral home to thrive. Today we host 10.

In "Who Keeps It Open?", Surtani argued that a license alone does not keep infrastructure open. Surtani contrasted Android, which stayed under one company, with Kubernetes, which Google moved into a neutral foundation. The open problems now sit in identity, attestation, audit, and payments.

Outside coverage was cooler. The New Stack noted that Open Responses already has support from AWS Bedrock, Databricks, Ollama, Nvidia, and vLLM, but that Anthropic still defines its own Messages API and Google its Interactions API. The Register headlined its story "Vendor-affiliated AI agent tech gets adopted by friendly, funded foundation" and closed with a caution:

This enthusiastic (or credulous) embrace of AI agents may be a bit too rapid for some industries.

J.R. Storment, executive director of the 11-week-old Tokenomics Foundation, told the audience to stop counting tokens. Cost per task beats cost per token, and cost per outcome is better still, but the real measure is business value.

David Soria Parra, co-creator of MCP at Anthropic, argued that capable models now need connectivity more than help staying on task. The July 28 specification added stateless servers, which some developers worried would turn MCP into just another API, and some platforms already see about 70% of their traffic in that mode. Soria Parra announced MCP tasks support in Claude Code, letting tool calls run for minutes, hours, or days instead of seconds. Anthropic also donated the Agent Skills standard to the foundation. The project's roadmap names five priority areas, from agent messaging and skills over MCP to identity and an HTTP-native transport.

OpenAI's Thomas Sarlandie shared what the ChatGPT plugin directory reveals about MCP servers in production. There is no practical limit on tool count, but oversized schemas get trimmed, starting with argument descriptions. About three in four tool schemas on published servers are under 1 kB, while the largest reach about 260 kB for a single tool and 1.4 MB for a server. OpenAI rejects submitted servers unless every tool carries annotations, which let ChatGPT fast-track read-only calls and confirm destructive ones. Only 56% of plugins use server instructions, which Sarlandie said can safely run to about 1,000 characters.

Chrome's Sarah Drasner presented WebMCP, a proposed web standard now in origin trial that lets websites expose tools to agents. Agents call declared tools instead of scraping the DOM, and Drasner cited benchmarks showing actions 2.5 to 7.5 times faster. Read-only and untrusted-content hints also help agents resist prompt injection hidden in user comments. WebMCP complements MCP rather than replacing it, Drasner stressed.

Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor, argued that frontier AI will help attackers more than defenders in the near term. Song's CyberGym benchmark spans more than 1,500 vulnerabilities in nearly 200 open source projects, and models now find zero-days. On ExploitGym, GPT-5.6 Sol produced about 230 working exploits against 869 targets in two hours, and still more than 80 with standard security mitigations enabled. Because attackers need only one hole, Song called for secure-by-construction systems with AI-generated proofs and pointed to a new observatory that tracks these capabilities.

Anthropic's Den Delimarsky, the protocol's lead maintainer, said cumulative SDK downloads have reached 4.17 billion. The count stood at about 3 billion a month earlier, which Delimarsky said raises the stakes of every security gap. About a third of the 116 conformance scenarios now test security, and enterprise-managed authorization is live in Claude. Delimarsky's auth roadmap marks that feature stable, puts proof-of-possession tokens and workload identity federation in draft, and ends with agents that sign in as themselves.

Block's Bradley Axen, creator of goose, demonstrated Buzz, an open source workspace where people and agents share channels. Each agent gets its own identity plus an attestation naming its owner, and can read channels but not direct messages. Buzz has 80,000 communities and 36,000 GitHub stars, with version 1.0 due in mid-November.

Thomas Dohmke, former GitHub CEO and now CEO of Entire, said agents have turned code review into the bottleneck. Citing industry data, Dohmke noted that teams using coding agents produce about 57 pull requests a week, against roughly 10 for others. Dohmke wants agent session logs stored in Git and linked to commits, so reviewers can check a change against its intent.

Tim O'Reilly called MCP an "architecture of participation" for AI, in the tradition of Unix. The AI economy still lacks its mechanisms, O'Reilly argued, much as the web needed pay-per-click advertising and secure payments. O'Reilly framed the fix as mechanism design, or "reverse game theory": start from the outcome you want and work backward to the rules that produce it. His message was to move trust out of the model and into protocols, gateways, and verifiable identity.

For teams running MCP servers, the practical lessons were specific: annotate every tool, keep schemas small, and plan for agents that carry their own identity rather than a borrowed user token. Several figures were stage claims without published data, and some security extensions remain drafts. Developers interested in learning more can watch the Day 1 and Day 2 keynote livestreams or read the foundation's project pages. The next AGNTCon + MCPCon events are set for San Francisco on April 28-29 and London on September 15-16, 2027.

entries.title: OpenTofu 1.13 Lets Module Authors Reduce Unknown Values at Plan Time
entries.summary: OpenTofu 1.13 adds convert and assume... functions that let module authors give the planner type and value hints for unknown values, so more expressions resolve during tofu plan. If a value unknown during planning later violates a guarantee, OpenTofu reports an error during apply. By Mark Silvester
entries.content:
OpenTofu released version 1.13 with functions that help module authors resolve more expressions during planning. Type and value hints can unblock plans when 

count
or the keys used by 
for_each
would otherwise remain unknown. The planner can determine how many resource instances to create without knowing all their eventual attributes, which can remain unknown until apply.

Martin Atkins, an OpenTofu maintainer, proposed the design in an RFC and merged the implementation in August. In an earlier issue, the reporter, csar398, wanted to retain YAML input but could not plan when the decoded value controlled 

count
. 
yamldecode
can return different types, including a null value, so an unknown input gives the planner neither a known type nor a non-null guarantee. Explaining the limitation, Atkins wrote: "... this is just too complex a situation for OpenTofu to infer automatically itself."

The 

convert
function converts values to a specified type, giving a 
yamldecode
result a known object type even when the YAML input is unknown. For conditional resources, combining that conversion with 
assumenotnull
lets a 
count
expression based on nullness resolve to zero or one while the object's contents remain unknown. The author must ensure that the generated YAML always represents an object of the specified type and never a null value. If a value unknown during planning later violates that guarantee, OpenTofu reports an error during apply.

Terraform shipped its equivalent 

convert
function first, in version 1.15. Atkins later wrote in an OpenTofu issue that "Terraform has an equivalent feature with syntax exactly like what I proposed here", and the project decided to match its design.

Experimental linting runs four built-in warning rules, including 

core:unused-variable
and 
core:count-instead-enabled
. The 
-lint=all
flag enables them with 
tofu validate
, 
tofu plan
or 
tofu apply
. In their linting proposal, the maintainers describe the feature as their most-voted request; future work covers custom rules and broader policy checks. TFLint already offers plugin-based static analysis, including cloud-provider checks.

The opt-in Symbol Libraries experiment shares functions and type definitions through 

*.sym.hcl
files. Libraries cannot directly access resources, data sources or provider functions, although callers can pass resource values into library functions. The team hopes to stabilise the feature in version 1.14.

Version 1.13 removes Windows Remote Management (WinRM) support from the 

remote-exec
and 
file
provisioners, changes 
base64gzip
output bytes, requires macOS 13 Ventura or later, and is the last series with official 32-bit builds. It also adds Windows on ARM64 packages. Existing WinRM configurations need migration, and the Go library change behind 
base64gzip
can trigger resource updates despite equivalent decompressed output.

OpenTofu shortened its development cycle to align with Go releases and supports the 1.13.x series until 1 August 2027. The project released version 1.13.2 on 21 October. Its two security changes address excessive CPU use during 

tofu init
when connecting to an attacker-controlled HTTP/2 server and filter compromised intermediate certificates. The patch also fixes applying saved plans that use symbol libraries.

entries.title: DigitalOcean Launches Learning and Data Services to Enable Self-Improving AI Agents
entries.summary: DigitalOcean has announced the public preview of Learning Services and Agent Data Services, enabling developers to build, evaluate, and continuously improve AI agents within a unified, AI-native, cloud platform. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
DigitalOcean has announced the public preview of Learning Services and Agent Data Services, enabling developers to build, evaluate, and continuously improve AI agents within a unified, AI-native, cloud platform.

The new services build on DigitalOcean's Inference Engine and Managed Agents to help agents learn from real-world interactions, identify weaknesses, test improvements, and leverage company data, the company says:

We built Inference Engine so agents could think, Managed Agents so they could act, and now Agent Learning Services and Agent Data Services so they can improve, on one open cloud and on the customer’s own data.

Learning Services combines three capabilities: Insights, which records agent activity; Signals, which identifies failures and performance gaps; and Simulations, which tests potential improvements through realistic conversations simulated before deployment.

Although separate from Learning Services, the enhanced Inference Router plays a key role in DigitalOcean's approach to continuously improving agents. It optimizes model selection based on task requirements, balances cost and quality, and reruns the same evaluations on new model versions.

Agent Data Services provides a secure, managed data foundation for AI agents. It processes and indexes documents, video, audio, logs, and agent sessions, making this information searchable and accessible through a unified catalog with built-in governance and access controls. It also integrates with Learning Services to support continuous agent improvement:

Agent Learning Services are built on [Data Services]: Signals writes sessions into it, and Optimizer draws its training and test data from it only where the customer expressly opts in.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedId, LakeOps co-founder Jonathan Saring observed:

The write-back loop is the part I find most interesting. Once traces, tool calls and outcomes feed evaluation or learning, they stop being “just logs” and become production data.

On a similar note, senior engineer Deepanshu Udhwani argued:

The write back what happened part is underrated compared to the read side everyone talks about with agent data layers. Most teams build great retrieval and skip logging outcomes properly, so six months later nobody can tell which tool calls actually worked versus which ones just looked fine in the moment.

Summarizing DigitalOcean's launch clip, TinyFish co-founder Keith Zhai, emphasized how Signals and Simulations can turn a failed user session into a fix before hundreds of other users encounter the same issue:

Signals and Simulations pull that session into a fix before the four-hundredth person hits the same wall. [...] Green tool calls next to abandoned users is still where most agent stacks break. The bottleneck is whether anyone can read the session the user actually lived.

DigitalOcean Insights, Signals, and Evaluations, including Simulations, are available in public preview. Inference Router optimization and Agent Data Services are available in private preview.

entries.title: Production AI and Engineering Team Design: InfoQ’s November Certification Cohorts
entries.summary: A preview of three November InfoQ online certification cohorts covering production AI systems, retrieval and agent design, engineering team flow, AI roles, and measurement, facilitated by Adi Polak, Lan Chu, and Olimpiu Pop. By Artenisa Chatziou
entries.content:
InfoQ has published details of three online certification cohorts starting in November 2026: AI Engineering with Adi Polak on November 12 (PST timezone), AI Engineering with Lan Chu on November 13 (CET timezone), and High-Performing Teams with Olimpiu Pop on November 17. The programs examine different parts of engineering work, from reliable retrieval and agent orchestration to delivery dependencies, human-AI responsibilities, and measures of team performance.

Production AI: Retrieval, Agents, and Operational Evidence

AI applications involve more than model selection. Retrieval can produce stale or incomplete context; more autonomous agents require decisions about control and verification; and shared AI infrastructure introduces questions about ownership and inference costs. The InfoQ Certified AI Engineering Program covers these decisions through work on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), context and memory pipelines, agent design, AI infrastructure, evaluations, and reliability.

Adi Polak, author of Scaling Machine Learning with Spark and an engineering leader who has built machine learning and real-time streaming pipelines, facilitates the November 12 cohort. Her syllabus uses QCon material on context engineering to compare vector retrieval with Graph RAG and considers how agents share state and context. Later weeks address orchestration, control, inference gateways, and rollout-readiness evaluations.

Lan Chu, a principal engineer with more than seven years of experience building production data and machine learning systems, facilitates the November 13 cohort. Her syllabus draws on her QCon London case study of a RAG system built on more than 10,000 documents and used by more than 300 people. The work includes tracing retrieval and indexing decisions, comparing vector retrieval with Graph RAG, evaluating single-agent against multi-agent designs, and selecting production-readiness checks. Each cohort follows its facilitator's published syllabus rather than an identical set of exercises.

Team Design When AI Changes the Flow of Work

Increasing the speed of code production does not necessarily shorten delivery time. Review, approvals, infrastructure dependencies, or rework may become the limiting step. Introducing AI agents also changes who prepares context, reviews output, and remains accountable for decisions. The InfoQ Certified High-Performing Teams Program examines these interactions as parts of one team operating model.

The November 17 cohort is facilitated by Olimpiu Pop, an InfoQ Podcast co-host with 20 years of experience across software architecture, engineering management, and technology leadership. Participants examine team boundaries and delivery flow, map dependencies, consider tasks delegated to AI alongside human judgment, and assess whether familiar output metrics remain informative. The group capstone develops and presents a target operating model connecting responsibilities, delivery flow, AI roles, and measurement.

Working Through Decisions with Practitioners from Other Companies

The cohorts bring together senior engineers and architects from other companies to apply material from QCon talks to current engineering decisions. Participants work with their facilitator in live online sessions, discuss the constraints behind different approaches, and return to the group with what happened when they applied the material. Sessions are not recorded. Each cohort includes four live hours per week plus up to two hours of independent work. Certification depends on participation and successful completion of the relevant capstone; selected work may be considered for InfoQ publication, but publication is not automatic.

Full dates, facilitator-specific syllabuses, and participation details are available on the InfoQ Online Certification Programs website.
